facts.fact: The debt snowball method pays off balances smallest-to-largest regardless of interest rate, prioritizing psychological momentum from quick wins.
facts.caveat: A behavioral strategy; may cost more in total interest than the avalanche method.

facts.fact: The debt avalanche method pays off balances highest-interest-rate-first, which minimizes total interest paid mathematically.
facts.caveat: Requires more discipline for some people since early wins take longer to see.

facts.fact: Making only the minimum payment on a credit card balance extends payoff time and increases total interest paid substantially compared to paying more than the minimum.
facts.caveat: Exact time/interest depends on the specific APR and balance; no single universal number applies.

facts.fact: Federal student loans in the U.S. offer income-driven repayment plans that tie the monthly payment to income and family size.
facts.caveat: Program details and availability change over time and by loan type; verify current rules before citing specifics.

facts.fact: Debt-to-income ratio (monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income) is a common metric lenders use to assess borrowing capacity.
facts.caveat: Specific lender thresholds vary by loan type and lender.

facts.fact: Consolidating several high-interest debts into a single lower-interest loan can simplify payments and reduce interest cost, if the borrower qualifies for a materially lower rate.
facts.caveat: Not guaranteed to save money if fees are high or the new rate isn't meaningfully lower.

facts.fact: Carrying a revolving balance does not help a credit score; utilization is measured off the reported balance regardless of whether it's paid in full or minimum.
facts.caveat: Common misconception worth myth-busting; see credit.json for utilization details.
